title: U.S. Solar Capacity Can Now Power Over 50 Million American Homes
gist: SEIA and Wood Mackenzie report 11.4 GWdc of US solar added in Q2 2026 (+45% YoY), with solar plus storage taking 70% of all new US grid capacity in H1 2026 and utility-scale contributing 9.6 GWdc as developers beat the July 2026 safe harbor deadline. The politically loaded detail: states Trump won in 2024 took 71% of H1 2026 installations and eight of the top ten spots.

insights.claim: Operating US solar capacity is now sufficient to power more than 50 million American homes, over one-third of all US households.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Solar has crossed from marginal to systemic in the US mix, which changes the political economics of rolling back support.
insights.locator: The United States now has enough operating solar capacity

insights.claim: Solar and storage together accounted for 70% of all new capacity added to the US grid in the first half of 2026.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: At 70% of new additions, solar-plus-storage is the default marginal supply technology — competing thermal capacity additions are now the exception.
insights.quote: Together, solar and storage account for 70% of all new capacity added to the grid in the first half of 2026.
insights.locator: Together, solar and storage account for 70%

insights.claim: SEIA CEO Tim Pawlenty argues the scale of US solar and storage is still not understood by most Americans and that growing energy needs cannot be met without those technologies.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Industry messaging is shifting from climate framing to energy-adequacy framing — a sign of how solar lobbying will be positioned in the post-ITC fight.
insights.quote: Solar and storage have grown to a scale most Americans have yet to fully realize and we simply can’t meet America’s growing energy needs without these technologies

insights.claim: The US solar industry added 11.4 GWdc of new generating capacity in Q2 2026, a 45% year-over-year increase and 43% above Q1.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Sets the baseline quarterly run-rate against which the post-safe-harbor slowdown will be measured.

insights.claim: Utility-scale solar installed 9.6 GWdc in Q2 2026, up 61% year-over-year, as developers rushed projects online ahead of the July 2026 safe harbor deadline for tax credit eligibility.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Deadline-driven volume inflates 2026 comparables; 2027 growth rates will look artificially weak against them.
insights.locator: Utility-scale solar led the Q2 surge

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's Caitlin Connelly says robust project pipelines and safe-harbored capacity will sustain roughly 44 GWdc of annual US solar capacity through 2031, with permitting and the post-ITC transition the significant headwinds.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A flat ~44 GWdc plateau is the number to anchor five-year demand models for modules, trackers and inverters.
insights.quote: Robust project pipelines and the build out of safe-harbored capacity will sustain roughly 44 GWdc of annual capacity through 2031
insights.locator: said Caitlin Connelly, senior analyst at Wood Mackenzie

insights.claim: The US solar market is forecast to nearly double over the next five years, positioning the industry as the fastest way to add large volumes of new power to meet rising demand.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Speed-to-power is becoming solar's core competitive argument against gas and nuclear in a demand-growth environment.
insights.locator: The report’s forecasts show that the U.S. solar market

insights.claim: Residential solar is expected to return to growth in 2027 after the expiration of the residential solar tax credit, driven by bill savings and resiliency rather than incentives.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: If residential demand is genuinely electricity-price-elastic rather than subsidy-driven, rising retail power prices become the bull case for installers into 2027.
insights.locator: The residential market continues to face challenges

insights.claim: States won by President Trump in 2024 accounted for 71% of all US solar capacity installed in the first half of 2026 and eight of the top ten states for new installations.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Solar's constituency is now concentrated in Republican districts, which materially lowers the political probability of an abrupt federal rollback — a key tail-risk discount for solar equities.
insights.quote: Solar is booming in states across the country, particularly in those won by President Trump in 2024, which accounted for 71% of all solar capacity installed in the first half of 2026
insights.locator: Solar is booming in states across the country
